title: Best Golf Push Trolleys UK
short: Six push trolleys tested on the course over varied terrain, compared on folding mechanism, weight and stability.
intro: A push trolley is the simplest, cheapest way to save your back and shoulders without the cost or weight of an electric model. This guide is based on Golf Monthly's tested roundup (updated July 2026), where reviewers took each trolley onto the course over several rounds in different conditions, from summer to winter and flat ground to hills, judging ease of use, manoeuvrability, robustness and value. No manufacturer receives preferential treatment.

products.name: Nitron Push Trolley
products.best_for: Golfers who want the quickest, easiest fold in a stable, feature-packed trolley
products.key_spec: 7.6kg, aluminium, single-step unfold, wide wheelbase, parking brake, bungee straps, phone holder
products.summary: Golf Monthly's top pick for ease of use and features. The folding mechanism is one of the quickest and easiest tested, unfolding in a single step and forming a compact unit once folded. At just over 7.5kg it's one of the lighter trolleys, easy in and out of a car boot, and a wide wheelbase makes it stable even on undulating terrain, with a parking brake, bungee straps and storage for balls, tees and a phone. The fixed wheel limits manoeuvrability somewhat, and the frame design is busy.
pros: Parking brake, bungee straps and phone/ball storage

products.name: Smart Fold Push Trolley
products.best_for: Golfers who want the simplest possible fold without paying a premium
products.key_spec: 7.2kg, aluminium, one-push-button fold, three-wheel design, umbrella and scorecard holders
products.summary: Golf Monthly found a superbly designed, affordable trolley: at 7.2kg it's easy to lift, and folding it is genuinely one of the more straightforward mechanisms around, needing just the push of a button. The three-wheel design gives plenty of stability on varying terrain, and adjustable brackets kept the bag secure even on hilly courses. It comes with a dry space for valuables, umbrella and scorecard holders and wheel covers, though it isn't the most compact once folded.
pros: One push of a button to fold
Super lightweight, holds a carry bag easily
cons: Not as compact as others when folded down
products.search: Eze Glide Smart Fold Push Trolley

products.name: Micra Push Trolley
products.best_for: Golfers who want strong looks matched with a genuinely compact fold
products.key_spec: 7.5kg, aluminium, two-click folding, three large wheels, Key Lock compatible with PowaKaddy bags
products.summary: Golf Monthly found form and function combined: a two-mechanism fold (handle moves down, wheels fold under the chassis) makes for a really compact unit that's easy to fit in a boot and store at home. It's easy to push thanks to an adjustable handle and three large wheels that eat up fairway and rough, and it's stable, with a water-resistant phone slot and holders for tees, balls, a scorecard and a pen. The Key Lock security system only works with a separate PowaKaddy bag.
pros: Glides easily across fairway and rough
cons: Key Lock system only useful with a separate PowaKaddy bag

products.name: QB2 Push Trolley
products.best_for: Golfers who want the smallest possible folded footprint for storage
products.key_spec: 9.5kg, aluminium, 20% smaller folded than the previous Cube, larger rear wheels, adjustable handle
products.summary: An update on Motocaddy's popular Cube trolley: the QB2 folds 20% smaller than its predecessor, making it truly compact to move and store despite being one of the heavier units tested. Larger rear wheels reduce friction for a genuinely easy push across fairways and rough, with a scorecard holder, accessories compartment and a handle net that suited holding a rangefinder. The narrower wheels make it a little less stable on tricky terrain, and the cube fold shape isn't for everyone.
pros: Folds even smaller than the previous version
Larger wheels make for an easier pushing experience
Adjustable handle suits any height golfer
cons: Cube folding shape isn't for everyone
Narrower wheels make it less stable on tricky terrain

products.name: Slimfold Push Trolley
products.best_for: Golfers who most value a fast, single-lever fold and slim storage
products.key_spec: 6.25kg, aluminium, single-lever fold, folded size 32.25 x 8.5 x 13.5in
products.summary: Golf Monthly calls this the best folding mechanism of the whole guide: a single lever unlocks the trolley to pull up or push down, with a bottom handle for extra leverage, making it as quick and straightforward as it gets. At just over 6kg it's a doddle in and out of the car, and its slim folded size makes storage easy. It performed admirably even with a heavy bag, though it isn't the smoothest or most stable trolley tested, and the storage pouch uses cheap material.
pros: Slim folded design makes transport and storage much easier
cons: Not the smoothest or most stable on course

products.name: Blade Trio Push Trolley
products.best_for: Golfers who want the lightest trolley to move around, paired with a lighter bag
products.key_spec: 6.7kg, aluminium, two-step folding mechanism, premium materials
products.summary: Golf Monthly found premium build quality despite weighing less than 7kg, and combined with a bag it felt the easiest of the group to move around, even slightly ahead of the marginally lighter Bag Boy Slimfold. The two-step fold is straightforward and space-saving, and on course it rolls along with little effort required, staying stable over tricky terrain despite a relatively narrow wheelbase. It's best suited to a lighter bag rather than a heavy tour-style model, and the rear wheelbase could be wider.
cons: Best suited to lighter bags rather than heavy tour bags
products.search: Big Max Blade Trio Push Trolley

guide.a: Push trolleys like these are cheaper, lighter, simpler to use and store, and need no charging, with better console storage for balls and tees. Electric trolleys need less effort to push and often add GPS or remote control, at a higher price and weight. See our separate electric golf trolleys guide for those.

Lighter trolleys are easier to lift in and out of a car boot. The Big Max Blade Trio (6.7kg) and Bag Boy Slimfold (6.25kg) are the lightest here, while the Motocaddy QB2 (9.5kg) is heavier but folds to the smallest footprint for storage.

Most push trolleys, including the PowaKaddy Micra and Eze Glide Smart Fold, use three wheels for a good balance of stability and manoeuvrability. A wider wheelbase, as on the Bag Boy Nitron, generally means more stability on undulating terrain, while narrower wheelbases can feel less stable on tricky ground.

guide.q: Will it suit a heavy tour-style bag?
guide.a: Check the wheelbase and build. Golf Monthly notes the Big Max Blade Trio suits a lighter bag rather than a heavy tour-style model, while the wider-wheelbase Bag Boy Nitron and PowaKaddy Micra coped well across varied terrain even loaded up.
